items.title: Mothers and fathers may pass along different kinds of sexism to their kids, new research suggests
items.summary: Fathers higher in hostile sexism tended to have children who agreed more with hostile statements about women, while mothers higher in benevolent sexism tended to have children who agreed more that women need men’s protection.

items.title: Two styles of meditation eased depressive symptoms in a four-week trial, possibly through different routes
items.summary: Not all meditation may work the same way. In a trial of 147 adults, focused-attention and self-inquiry meditation produced similar drops in depressive symptoms, but exploratory analyses pointed to different underlying processes.

items.title: Weaker inputs to a key emotion hub are linked to more depressive symptoms in healthy young adults
items.summary: Young adults with weaker incoming connections to the subgenual anterior cingulate cortex, a small region that helps regulate emotion, tended to report more depressive symptoms, according to brain scans of 890 healthy volunteers.

items.title: Unhealthy daily habits cluster together to predict adolescent anxiety and depression
items.summary: A large study reveals that unhealthy habits like excessive screen time and poor diet tend to group together in teenagers. These behavioral clusters strongly predict the future onset of combined anxiety and depression.

items.title: Women with high cognitive ability tend to be seen as more hostile by teammates and report more mistreatment
items.summary: Highly intelligent women often face a hidden social penalty in the workplace. A new study reveals that female employees with high cognitive ability are perceived as more hostile, leading to fewer supportive interactions with their colleagues.

items.title: Learning to read may shape how adults reason about what others believe
items.summary: Can learning to read change how we think about other people’s minds? Among 76 Turkish women, reading fluency was the strongest predictor of performance on a test of reasoning about what one person thinks another believes.

items.title: Weak handgrip strength linked to higher risk of depression over time
items.summary: A massive new review of medical data reveals that lower handgrip strength is linked to a higher risk of developing depression over time, suggesting physical strength may serve as an early indicator of general health and mental vulnerability.

items.title: Scientists identify DNA regions tied to binge eating, including one near a well-known obesity gene
items.summary: Binge eating and anorexia are genetically linked to opposite ends of the body weight spectrum, but a study of more than 1.2 million people found both share genetic ties to depression, anxiety, and schizophrenia.

items.title: How public opinion on transgender bathroom access shifted between 2016 and 2022
items.summary: Public opinion on transgender bathroom access has grown more conservative since 2016. A new study reveals how Americans weigh competing arguments about safety and discrimination, and why conflicted voters increasingly support restrictive policies.

items.title: Nostalgia for a party’s past cuts both ways when it comes to support for political violence
items.summary: Nostalgia for a party’s past doesn’t mean the same thing to every partisan. Partisans who felt nostalgic reported more support for violence if their passion was obsessive, but less if it was harmonious.

items.title: New compounds target clumping enzyme to protect brain cells in Alzheimer’s models
items.summary: An enzyme called GRK2 clumps up and damages cellular powerhouses in the brains of mice with Alzheimer's disease. Newly developed chemical compounds that prevent or eliminate these clumps helped preserve memory and slow brain cell death in the animals.

items.title: Weight loss medications alter how the brain and kidneys manage body fluids
items.summary: Medications like liraglutide help treat diabetes and obesity, but they also cause water loss. A new study reveals how these drugs directly lower levels of a key water-conserving hormone, altering chemical signals from the brain to the kidneys.

items.title: Why is autism increasing? Scientists are converging on an unglamorous answer
items.summary: Autism diagnoses have skyrocketed over the past few decades, prompting a debate among scientists. Is the biological rate of autism actually rising, or is society simply naming the condition more frequently?

items.title: Sleep loss reduces muscle endurance by rewiring brain networks, study finds
items.summary: Getting less than four hours of sleep severely reduces physical endurance, but not because your muscles tire out faster. A new study shows that sleep deprivation forces the brain to inefficiently rewire its neural networks, triggering premature physical exhaustion.

items.title: Psilocybin therapy has mostly reached the well-off. A small Oregon study tested a cheaper group model for low-income patients
items.summary: Most psychedelic research has drawn well-off participants. In a first-of-its-kind Oregon study, 19 low-income adults with depression completed group psilocybin therapy, and their average depression scores fell by more than half.

items.title: Hiring bias against transgender women depends on both identity and appearance, field experiment suggests
items.summary: In a field experiment involving more than 10,000 job applications in Germany, trans women who disclosed their identity or had male-coded facial features each received about 10 percent fewer positive responses from employers. When both signals were present, the penalty jumped to 32 percent.

items.title: Many people judge candidates and policies by a single deciding feature, new research suggests
items.summary: Many survey methods assume people weigh every feature of a candidate or policy. New research suggests most don’t: mental shortcuts dominated, and the strategy people used often shifted from one issue to the next.

items.title: Oxytocin amplifies negative childhood memories for anxiously attached adults
items.summary: Oxytocin is often called the "love hormone," but new research shows it can actually amplify negative childhood memories for people who experience relationship anxiety. The hormone appears to heighten our sensitivity to social cues, rather than simply boosting affection.

items.title: Some adults’ brains look older than their age, and gut biology may be part of the picture
items.summary: Some adults’ brains look “older” than their age long before old age. In a study of 1,400+ people aged 18 to 65, older-looking brain patterns were linked to somewhat weaker working memory, more depressive symptoms, and subtle gut differences.

items.title: Family genetics study questions the role of genetic nurture in ADHD
items.summary: A large study of families suggests that a child's own DNA drives their ADHD traits by mid-childhood, finding no robust evidence that parents' genetics indirectly shape these behaviors through the household environment.

items.title: Scientists discover how deep sleep builds muscle, burns fat, and boosts the brain
items.summary: Scientists have discovered a surprising two-way relationship between sleep and growth hormone, revealing how the brain carefully balances physical recovery with wakefulness. The findings could help explain why poor sleep harms metabolism and brain health, potentially opening the door to new treatments for sleep and neurological disorders.

items.title: Mysterious brain activity under anesthesia challenges what we know about consciousness
items.summary: Even under general anesthesia, the human brain can analyze language, recognize different types of words, and predict what comes next in a story, according to a surprising discovery by Baylor researchers. The findings challenge our understanding of consciousness and suggest that the unconscious brain is far more capable than scientists previously realized.

items.title: Yale scientists discover how stress changes the brain to make memories stronger
items.summary: Yale scientists have uncovered how the stress hormone cortisol helps the brain turn emotional experiences into stronger, longer-lasting memories. The discovery reveals that stress can reshape communication between brain networks involved in emotion and memory, potentially explaining why certain moments are so difficult to forget.

items.title: The secret to handling stress better may start at breakfast
items.summary: Your daily routine could have a bigger impact on your ability to handle stress than you realize. A Binghamton University study of approximately 400 college students found that eating breakfast regularly, exercising, sleeping well, and taking fish oil were associated with greater psychological flexibility, which helps people adapt to stressful situations. Poor sleep and unhealthy eating habits, mea

items.title: Scientists uncover a hidden map of the brain with 539 distinct regions
items.summary: Scientists have uncovered a hidden layer of organization in the brain by creating the first detailed 3D map of its lipids, the fatty molecules essential for brain structure and communication. By analyzing millions of measurements from mouse brains, researchers identified 539 distinct chemical zones, revealing patterns and boundaries that traditional brain maps have missed. Surprisingly, even white

items.title: Scientists find hidden driver of aging and a simple amino acid that fights memory loss in mice
items.summary: Scientists discovered that declining levels of a protein called Menin may help drive aging, and restoring it in older mice reversed several age-related changes in just 30 days. Even more surprisingly, supplementing with a simple amino acid called D-serine improved memory and learning, offering a potential new approach to age-related cognitive decline.

items.title: Just 10 minutes of daily exercise could unlock deeper sleep
items.summary: Getting better sleep might be as simple as moving a little more every day. Researchers at The University of Texas at Austin found that people who exercised more frequently experienced more deep, restorative sleep, which is essential for brain recovery, memory, and emotional well-being. Surprisingly, just 10 minutes of moderate to vigorous exercise per day was associated with measurable benefits, w

items.title: Scientists discover 5 hidden brain patterns behind depression
items.summary: Depression may not be one biological condition, but several distinct patterns of brain activity hiding under the same diagnosis. Researchers studying 263 people with depression identified five brain profiles, each showing different patterns of communication between brain regions and associations with symptoms such as anxiety, trauma, and substance abuse.

items.title: After 30 years, scientists finally have a drug for a deadly brain disease
items.summary: The FDA has approved the first drug that directly targets Alexander disease, a devastating neurological disorder affecting fewer than one in a million people. Developed through decades of research, Zanvastro showed promising results in clinical trials, stabilizing motor function and even improving movement in some patients.

items.title: Loneliness may steal nearly 6 years of good health
items.summary: A large study suggests loneliness and social isolation can cost people years of healthy life, especially when it comes to mental health. Men experiencing both lost about 5.8 years free from depression and anxiety, while women lost roughly 3.7 years.

items.title: Drug target could block brain inflammation linked to Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s
items.summary: Blocking a receptor called P2X7 significantly reduced inflammation in human brain tissue, revealing a potential new treatment strategy for neurological and psychiatric disorders. The discovery could help researchers repurpose existing drugs for conditions including traumatic brain injury, Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s, depression, and schizophrenia.

items.title: What happens in the brain when cannabis makes you anxious?
items.summary: Cannabinoids may intensify anxiety by removing a natural brake on specific neurons in the brain’s fear center, particularly during stressful situations. In mice, shutting down those neurons sharply reduced cannabinoid-related anxious behavior.

items.title: Vagus Nerve Stimulation Could Help New Skills Stick
items.summary: Stimulating the vagus nerve after practice helped mice develop stronger long-term motor learning, revealing a potentially important window when the brain is still locking in a new skill. The effect was linked to rhythmic changes in brain blood vessels, hinting that body-to-brain signals may help prepare the brain for lasting change.

items.title: This diet may slow brain aging by 2.5 years
items.summary: People who followed the MIND diet more closely showed slower brain shrinkage and less grey matter loss over time, with the strongest differences equivalent to about 2.5 years of delayed brain aging. Berries and poultry were linked with healthier brain changes, while sweets and fried fast foods were associated with greater tissue loss.

items.title: Could quitting ultra-processed food boost your mental health?
items.summary: People with depression who dramatically cut ultra-processed foods experienced notable improvements in their symptoms in a small preliminary study. Researchers suspect healthier eating may benefit the brain partly by reducing gut damage and chronic inflammation.

items.title: Brain scans reveal which disorders are linked to faster brain aging
items.summary: A massive MRI study found that Alzheimer’s disease, mild cognitive impairment, psychiatric disorders, and addiction are associated with distinct patterns of accelerated brain aging. The strongest effects appeared in Alzheimer’s and mild cognitive impairment, while ADHD and autism showed no significant overall difference.

items.title: Children at risk for depression get “stuck” on sad faces
items.summary: Depression may change which emotional faces children notice most, but the pattern appears to depend on family history. Children at higher familial risk became increasingly focused on sad faces, while lower-risk children with rising symptoms paid less attention to happy ones.

items.title: Scientists just discovered what coffee really does to your gut and brain
items.summary: A new study suggests coffee may influence mood and brain function by changing the activity of microbes in the gut. Both caffeinated and decaf coffee were linked to lower stress, depression, and impulsivity, while also producing measurable changes in gut bacteria and metabolites. items.title: When what you see doesn’t make sense, your brain does something remarkable
items.summary: The brain may have a built-in way to quickly settle disagreements between regions processing the same scene. Researchers found that matching signals between two visual areas lasted longer, while conflicting signals rapidly faded away. This “consensus building” mechanism could help explain how the brain turns many specialized inputs into one unified view of the world.

items.title: Coffee doesn’t have to keep you awake to disrupt your sleep
items.summary: Caffeine may make sleep less restorative even when you fall asleep normally and stay in bed for eight hours, with EEG recordings revealing fewer of the slow brain waves associated with deep sleep. Individual sensitivity varies dramatically, meaning even caffeine consumed earlier in the day could affect nighttime recovery for some people.

items.title: Scientists create a needle-thin brain implant that can do three jobs at once
items.summary: A new needle-thin brain implant can record neural activity, deliver drugs, and stimulate multiple brain regions using a single flexible fiber. Successful tests in mice suggest it could give scientists a more precise, less invasive way to study the brain and may eventually help treat neurological disorders such as epilepsy.

items.title: Scientists restore a brain protein and reverse signs of aging in mice
items.summary: Scientists found that declining levels of the brain protein Menin may help drive aging, with lower levels in mice linked to inflammation, cognitive decline, weaker bones, and thinner skin. Restoring Menin reversed several age-related changes, while the amino acid D-serine improved cognition, hinting at a potentially intriguing new target for healthy aging.

items.title: Hidden brain wiring may help keep the mind sharp as gray matter shrinks
items.summary: Scientists have discovered that the brain’s short-range wiring may help protect cognition even as gray matter shrinks with age. Healthier connections just beneath the brain’s surface were linked to better language skills and appeared to weaken the impact of gray matter loss.

items.title: Scientists find a new layer of Alzheimer’s hidden in the genome
items.summary: Scientists found that the 3D organization of DNA is disrupted in several types of brain cells affected by Alzheimer’s disease, altering how important genes are switched on and off. The discovery reveals a previously underexplored layer of the disease that could open new paths for understanding and eventually treating Alzheimer’s.

items.title: A longer exhale may push your brain toward bolder decisions
items.summary: Slow breathing with a prolonged exhale made people more willing to take risks by changing heart activity and increasing the brain’s sensitivity to rewards. The findings suggest that something as simple as controlling your breath can directly influence how you evaluate choices.

items.title: Scientists reveal the hidden instructions that build the human brain
items.summary: UCLA researchers have discovered two powerful influences that help guide how the human brain forms before birth. Radial glia, stem cells responsible for producing much of the cerebral cortex, change their behavior depending on how they process glucose and on physical contact with signals arriving from the thalamus. items.title: HEPA air purifiers may boost brain function after just one month
items.summary: Adults aged 40 and older performed about 12% faster on a test of executive function after using a HEPA air purifier at home for one month. The findings suggest that cleaner indoor air could offer a simple way to help protect the brain from the effects of traffic-related pollution.

items.title: Scientists challenge a 70-year-old “lizard brain” myth
items.summary: A long-standing picture of brain evolution as newer, rational layers stacked on top of an ancient “lizard brain” may be deeply misleading. Researchers found that evolution instead appears to balance two competing styles of brain wiring, expanding one while shrinking the other depending on what an animal needs to survive.

items.title: Too much or too little sleep may make your body age faster
items.summary: Both too little and too much sleep may be linked to faster aging throughout the body. Researchers analyzing 23 biological aging clocks found the lowest aging levels among people sleeping about 6.4 to 7.8 hours per day. Short or long sleep was also associated with numerous conditions affecting the brain, heart, lungs, metabolism, and digestive system.

items.title: Childhood trauma may leave a lasting “scar” inside brain cells
items.summary: Early-life stress may physically alter how DNA is packaged in the brain, leaving stress-related genes primed to activate more easily years later. In mice, researchers were able to block this effect, preventing the heightened anxiety and stress sensitivity that otherwise appeared in adulthood.

items.title: Your brain may not actually “make” decisions
items.summary: A neuroscientist is challenging the idea that the brain contains a central system that actually “makes” our decisions. What we experience as choosing may instead emerge from the continuous interaction of perception, movement, the body, and the world around us.

items.title: Depression may shut down the brain’s ability to make new neurons
items.summary: A major study found that adults with depression show disrupted production of new neurons in the hippocampus, potentially weakening the brain’s ability to separate new experiences from painful memories. The researchers also identified broad molecular changes that could open the door to new treatments tailored to different biological forms of depression.

items.title: A major Alzheimer’s risk gene may shrink brain cells years before symptoms
items.summary: Researchers have uncovered a possible reason why the Alzheimer’s risk gene APOE4 can disrupt the brain long before memory problems begin. In mice, APOE4 increased a protein called Nell2, shrinking neurons and making memory circuits unusually active. That early hyperactivity predicted worse memory later in life. items.title: Schizophrenia’s lost brain connections follow a surprising pattern
items.summary: Specialized brain scans reveal that schizophrenia is linked to widespread loss of the synapses that connect brain cells, with the left side of the brain hit especially hard. The damage follows a surprisingly organized pattern tied to the brain’s chemistry and wiring. Researchers also identified a left frontal region that may serve as a starting point for the loss.

items.title: Scientists reveal how the brain changes its connections when uncertainty strikes
items.summary: The brain has a remarkably flexible system for handling uncertainty and changing situations. Researchers found that the frontoparietal cortex constantly shifts how it communicates with other brain regions depending on what information is needed to make a decision. Rather than simply becoming more active when things get difficult, this network appears to reorganize itself in real time.

items.title: A therapy that “rewrites” childhood memories can ease fear of failure
items.summary: Childhood criticism can leave people carrying a fear of failure long into adulthood, but new research suggests those emotional patterns may be surprisingly flexible. Young adults who revisited painful memories through imagery-based therapy showed lasting reductions in fear, guilt, sadness, and stress.

items.title: A little-known protein may be fueling Alzheimer’s — and scientists found a way to block it
items.summary: An experimental Alzheimer’s compound prevented damaging protein clumps from forming in the brains of mice, helping nerve cells survive longer and reducing amyloid buildup. The treatment also appeared to improve heart health and slow some signs of aging, raising hopes for an entirely new way to combat dementia.

items.title: A stress hormone may help the brain repair itself
items.summary: A surprising stress-related signal may help the brain repair itself after injury. Researchers found that myelin-producing precursor cells rapidly release the stress hormone CRH near damaged brain tissue, helping control how those cells mature and rebuild protective nerve insulation. items.title: Scientists discover a hidden brain rhythm that could improve Parkinson’s treatment
items.summary: Scientists have pinpointed a brain network—and its distinctive electrical rhythm—that appears to drive the benefits of deep brain stimulation for Parkinson’s disease. The discovery could lead to more precise, personalized stimulation settings and better results for patients.

items.title: Ozempic may have revealed the brain’s hidden “craving center”
items.summary: Ozempic-like drugs appear to weaken more than hunger—they may also reduce cravings for alcohol and other addictive substances. Scientists are increasingly tracing this effect to the lateral septum, a brain region that helps connect memories and surroundings with rewarding experiences. items.title: Frequent cannabis users wake up with their “stress hormone” already elevated
items.summary: Frequent cannabis users may wake up with unusually high levels of the stress hormone cortisol, suggesting their daily stress rhythms could be disrupted. Researchers say the finding raises questions about whether using cannabis for stress relief might, over time, interfere with the very system that helps the body handle stress.

items.title: Stress can scramble your brain’s internal GPS, MRI study finds
items.summary: Stress may literally scramble the brain’s internal GPS. Researchers found that cortisol, a hormone released during stress, made people significantly worse at navigating a virtual environment and disrupted the precise activity of grid cells, specialized brain cells that help us understand where we are in space. When landmarks were missing, this navigation system nearly stopped functioning, while an

items.title: Scientists tracked 12 people in Antarctica for 10 months—what happened could shape future Mars missions
items.summary: A ten-month Antarctic experiment found that astronauts may struggle not only with loneliness but also with spending too much time around the same people. Frequent contact was linked to greater tension and mistrust, while the crew increasingly divided into cultural and language-based groups.

items.title: Wearable ultrasound patch boosts REM sleep without drugs or surgery
items.summary: A new wearable patch may help people reach REM sleep faster and remain there longer without medication or surgery. In a study of 28 participants, the device shortened the time to REM by 43 minutes and extended it by about 16 minutes. Researchers also observed signs of improved stress regulation and changes in brain circuits tied to emotion.

items.title: THC medication made PTSD nightmares disappear for more than a third of patients
items.summary: A prescription form of THC helped many people with PTSD escape recurring trauma-related nightmares, with more than one-third reporting that the nightmares disappeared completely after ten weeks. The results could point toward a long-awaited treatment for one of PTSD’s most distressing and stubborn symptoms.

items.title: Nearly half of dementia cases may be linked to risks you can change
items.summary: A long-term brain study found that common risks such as smoking, high blood pressure, heart disease, and high blood lipids were strongly linked to damage associated with vascular dementia. The findings suggest that healthier lifestyle choices could help delay dementia by reducing several harmful brain changes at once.

items.title: AI can tell if your brain is aging faster than you are
items.summary: A person’s sleeping brain may reveal warning signs of dementia long before memory problems begin. Researchers used machine learning to analyze EEG recordings from about 7,000 adults and found that an older-than-expected “brain age” was tied to a sharply higher dementia risk. Every additional 10 years of brain aging raised that risk by nearly 40%.

items.title: Scientists discover why poor sleep may harm some brains more
items.summary: A gene involved in the brain’s overnight cleaning system may change how strongly poor sleep affects Alzheimer’s-related brain changes. The findings point toward more personalized prevention strategies based on both genetics and sleep habits.

items.title: Your gut may help your brain decide what to remember
items.summary: Signals traveling from the gut to the brain may help turn meals into lasting memories. Rats showed stronger memory activity after consuming nutritious foods, but not after drinking sweet liquids with little or no nutritional value. Blocking the vagus nerve erased this effect and made it harder for the animals to remember where food had been located. Over time, diets high in fat and sugar also weak

items.title: Scientists find a simple routine linked to less pain and depression
items.summary: Keeping a regular daily schedule may help reduce pain and depression, especially among older adults with insomnia. Researchers found that consistent times for waking, eating, socializing, and sleeping were linked to better well-being regardless of sleep quality. These routines may strengthen the body’s internal clock and limit the disruptive effects of “social jet lag.”

items.title: Inside the Backrooms: The internet’s creepiest place is becoming a tourist attraction
items.summary: The Backrooms began as a single eerie image of empty yellow rooms, but internet users transformed it into a vast fictional world that feels disturbingly real. Through videos, games, maps, survival guides and social media stories, audiences do more than watch the horror unfold. They help build and explore it. items.title: APOE2 may protect the brain from Alzheimer’s and aging
items.summary: The longevity-linked APOE2 gene appears to protect brain cells by reducing DNA damage and helping neurons recover from stress. The finding could open a new path toward treatments that mimic APOE2’s defenses in people at higher genetic risk for Alzheimer’s.

items.title: Lab-grown mini brains may predict which Alzheimer’s treatments will work
items.summary: Miniature brain models grown from patients’ cells revealed striking differences in how Alzheimer’s-related tissue responds to an antidepressant. The organoids and the particles they release could eventually guide more personalized treatments and provide new clues for diagnosing the disease.

items.title: Watching too much TV in midlife may shrink the brain
items.summary: Watching television very often in midlife may be linked to troubling brain changes decades later. In a study of about 1,700 adults, frequent TV viewers later showed smaller brain regions involved in memory, decision-making, and visual processing, along with more signs of damage in the brain’s white matter. items.title: Magic mushrooms may reshape the brain long after the trip ends
items.summary: A single dose of psilocybin produced measurable changes in brain activity and possible changes in brain structure that lasted for up to a month. Participants who experienced the greatest increase in flexible, varied brain activity also reported more personal insight and later improvements in well-being. The findings suggest that the psychedelic experience itself may help people break free from ent

items.title: Alzheimer’s breakthrough: Scientists restore two hours of sleep without clearing brain plaques
items.summary: Researchers have uncovered a surprising culprit behind sleep loss in Alzheimer’s disease: the brain’s own immune cells. In mice with amyloid plaques, overactive microglia triggered inflammation that kept the brain from getting enough deep, restorative sleep. Temporarily removing most of these cells restored more than two hours of sleep per day, even though the plaques remained unchanged.

items.title: Mediterranean diet may activate tiny proteins that protect the heart and brain
items.summary: The Mediterranean diet may influence aging through tiny proteins produced inside the cell’s mitochondria. Older adults who followed the diet most closely had higher levels of humanin and SHMOOSE, which have been linked to heart and brain protection. items.title: Going to museums, movies, and theater may help your body stay younger
items.summary: Going to the cinema, visiting museums, or attending concerts may do more than entertain. Researchers found that older adults who regularly participated in cultural activities tended to have bodies that functioned like those of people about three years younger. They believe stronger social ties, better mental health, and healthier habits could help explain the link, although more research is needed

items.title: Scientists discover how the brain rewires itself to truly multitask
items.summary: Practice may do more than make perfect. Researchers found that extensive training physically reorganizes the brain, allowing learned tasks to bypass the prefrontal cortex and run through specialized circuits instead. items.title: Scientists discovered the brain doesn't make decisions the way we thought
items.summary: A new study suggests the brain begins making decisions much earlier than scientists previously thought. Researchers found that even primary sensory regions are influenced by higher brain areas through rapid feedback loops, rather than simply passing information forward. items.summary: Nature Human Behaviour, Published online: 12 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41562-026-02611-4 Simulating a global survey of economic preferences across 74 countries, this study shows that large language models reproduce some demographic patterns in human preferences but fail to capture cultural differences, especially in lower-income countries.

items.title: Recreational screen use and internalizing problems from preadolescence to young adulthood in a longitudinal twin cohort with co-twin comparison
items.summary: Nature Human Behaviour, Published online: 08 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41562-026-02607-0 Using longitudinal twin data, this study finds that associations between youth recreational screen use and internalizing problems are substantially reduced within twin pairs, suggesting shared familial contributions to the observed association.

items.title: Microdelays disrupt online learning
items.summary: Nature Human Behaviour, Published online: 08 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41562-026-02598-y Analysing data from more than 80,000 students and aspiring coders, Mazar et al. show that microdelays, brief loading lags caused by slow internet connections, can impair online learning.

items.title: Algorithm-assisted personalized risk communication to encourage flu vaccination in the USA: three randomized field trials
items.summary: Nature Human Behaviour, Published online: 05 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41562-026-02603-4 Rosenbaum et al. show that targeted communications highlighting patients’ high-risk status increased influenza vaccination uptake. However, they did not find an additional effect of informing patients that a computer algorithm was used to identify their risk status.
